plan: SAT R&W batch 73: 20 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000664..000683, weighted toward Standard English Conventions (10 SEC: Drew relative-clause agreement, electric-eel semicolon series, bombardier beetle agreement, beaver conjunctive adverb, elaiosome parallelism, bobtail squid relative-pronoun agreement, Arctic tern logical comparison, Augusta Savage whom, Joplin sales agreement, Lomax indirect question), plus Kahlo and Edmonia Lewis WIC, Darwin orchid structure, Green Sahara cross-text (Wright), Maria Martinez inference, krill quantitative trend, saguaro shade evidence, Hanseatic and Jacob Lawrence transitions, and Ellington synthesis. Topics checked against both workstreams. Plus S072-20 (revision 2) on its previously unbanked passage. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Banking blood
passages.text: In 1940, the surgeon Charles Drew directed Blood for Britain, a program that collected blood in New York and shipped its liquid plasma to treat wounded soldiers and civilians in Britain. Drew, whose research on separating and storing plasma ______ make large-scale blood banks practical, went on to lead the first American Red Cross blood bank the following year.

passages.title: Three kinds of shocks
passages.text: Biologist Kenneth Catania found that electric eels use their electricity in at least three ways: low-voltage pulses, to sense objects in murky ______ high-voltage pulses, to stun prey; and rapid pairs of high-voltage pulses, to make hidden prey twitch and reveal itself.

passages.title: A chemical defense
passages.text: When threatened, a bombardier beetle mixes chemicals stored in two separate chambers of its abdomen, triggering a reaction that releases a burst of spray. The spray, which the beetle can aim in almost any direction, ______ nearly as hot as boiling water.

passages.title: Water for dry seasons
passages.text: By damming streams, beavers create ponds that store water long after rainstorms have passed. Beaver ponds can hold water through dry ______ they can help keep downstream areas wet during droughts.

passages.title: Seeds with a snack
passages.text: Many plants, such as trilliums and bloodroot, attach a small fatty structure called an elaiosome to their seeds. Ants carry the seeds back to their nests, feed the elaiosomes to their larvae, and then ______ the seeds in underground waste piles, where they can sprout.

passages.title: A light to hide by
passages.text: The Hawaiian bobtail squid hunts in shallow water at night, when moonlight could cast its shadow onto the sand below. To hide that shadow, the squid relies on light produced by colonies of a bacterium, Vibrio fischeri, that ______ inside a special organ on its underside.

passages.title: Pole to pole
passages.text: Tracking devices have shown that some Arctic terns fly roughly 70,000 kilometers each year as they travel between breeding grounds in the Arctic and feeding areas near Antarctica. This yearly round trip is longer than ______ of any other animal known to science.

passages.title: A mentor in Harlem
passages.text: In 1932, the sculptor Augusta Savage opened the Savage Studio of Arts and Crafts in Harlem, offering free classes to anyone who wanted to learn. Savage, ______ many young artists of the Harlem Renaissance regarded as their mentor, went on to become the first director of the Harlem Community Art Center.

passages.title: The king of ragtime
passages.text: Scott Joplin's "Maple Leaf Rag," published in 1899, became one of the best-known pieces of American music of its time. Joplin had arranged to receive a royalty of one cent on each copy sold, and sales of the sheet music ______ strong enough to provide him with a modest but steady income for years.

passages.title: Questions for the singers
passages.text: In the 1930s, the folklorist Alan Lomax traveled across the American South recording musicians for the Library of Congress. Before he turned on his recording machine, Lomax often asked the musicians where they had learned their ______

passages.title: Self-portraits without flattery
passages.text: Frida Kahlo painted about fifty-five self-portraits, and they are rarely ______: she showed her joined eyebrows and the faint hair above her lip without softening them, and in several works she depicted the injuries and surgeries that shaped her life.

passages.title: Cleopatra after death
passages.text: Most earlier artists who depicted Cleopatra showed her in the moments before her death, often with the snake raised to strike. Edmonia Lewis's marble sculpture The Death of Cleopatra, shown at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, instead presented the queen after she had died. Lewis's approach was ______ for its time.

passages.title: A moth foretold
passages.text: In 1862, Charles Darwin examined an orchid from Madagascar whose nectar lay at the bottom of a tube nearly a foot long. He predicted that some moth must have a tongue long enough to reach it and thus pollinate the flower. No such moth was known at the time, and some scientists doubted it existed. In 1903, entomologists described a Madagascan hawk moth with a tongue long enough to reach the nectar.

passages.title: When the Sahara was green
passages.text:
Text 1
Between about 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, much of the Sahara was covered by grasslands and lakes. Most researchers attribute the end of this "Green Sahara" to gradual changes in Earth's orbit that weakened the summer monsoon rains over northern Africa.

Text 2
Archaeologist David Wright has argued that people also played a role. As herders spread across the region with cattle, sheep, and goats, he suggests, grazing and burning may have reduced plant cover and so sped up the drying that was already under way.

passages.title: A potter's signature
passages.text: Maria Martinez, a potter from San Ildefonso Pueblo in New Mexico, became famous for her polished black-on-black pottery, which she developed with her husband, Julian, around 1918. As collectors' interest grew, she began signing her pots in the 1920s. Martinez sometimes also signed pots that had been made by other women of the pueblo. This practice suggests that ______

passages.title: Krill and winter ice
passages.text:
Antarctic krill larvae feed on algae that grow on the underside of sea ice. A student compared summer krill counts in three study areas with the number of months each area had been covered by sea ice the previous winter.
Area 1: 5 months of ice; 42 krill per cubic meter
Area 2: 2 months of ice; 18 krill per cubic meter
Area 3: 0 months of ice; 6 krill per cubic meter
The student claims that the longer an area had been covered by sea ice in winter, the more krill it had the following summer.

passages.title: A shady start
passages.text: Young saguaro cacti in the Sonoran Desert are often found growing beneath trees such as palo verdes, which ecologists call nurse plants. Some ecologists hypothesize that nurse plants help young saguaros survive mainly by shading them from intense sunlight.

passages.title: Merchants of the north
passages.text: For several centuries, the Hanseatic League, an alliance of merchant towns such as Lübeck and Hamburg, dominated trade in the Baltic and North Seas. Its merchants enjoyed special privileges in foreign trading centers such as London and Bergen. ______ by the 1500s, the league's power had begun to fade as Dutch and English traders competed for the same routes and as stronger national governments challenged its privileges.

passages.title: Painted all at once
passages.text: In 1940 and 1941, Jacob Lawrence completed his Migration Series, sixty small panels depicting the movement of African Americans from the rural South to northern cities. Rather than finishing one panel before starting the next, Lawrence worked on all sixty at once, applying a single color to every panel where it was needed before moving on to the next color. ______ the series has a striking visual unity, with the same few colors repeated from panel to panel.

passages.title: Notes on a bandleader
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Duke Ellington (1899–1974) led one of the most celebrated orchestras in American music.
- He composed more than a thousand works, including "Mood Indigo" (1930).
- In 1965, a Pulitzer Prize jury recommended a special award for Ellington, but the Pulitzer board declined to give it.
- In 1999, the Pulitzer board awarded Ellington a special citation, twenty-five years after his death.

passages.title: Notes on a variable star
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Henrietta Swan Leavitt worked at the Harvard College Observatory in the early 1900s.
- She studied Cepheid variable stars, which brighten and dim on a regular cycle.
- In 1912, she reported that brighter Cepheids have longer cycles.
- Because of this relationship, a Cepheid's cycle reveals its true brightness, and comparing true brightness with how bright it appears reveals its distance.
- In the 1920s, Edwin Hubble used Cepheids to show that some galaxies lie far beyond the Milky Way.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: whose research on separating and storing plasma
candidates.explanation: In the clause "whose research ... helped make," the subject is the singular "research," and the events are in the past, so "helped" is correct.

A.rationale: "Help" does not agree with the singular "research" and does not fit the past events.

B.rationale: The plural verb does not agree with the singular "research."

D.rationale: "Helping" leaves the relative clause without a verb.

hints: What is the subject of the verb inside the "whose" clause?

strategy.explanation: Find the subject of the clause, not the nearest noun.

candidates.remember: Agree the verb with its subject inside a relative clause too.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: high-voltage pulses, to stun prey; and rapid pairs
candidates.explanation: The items in this series contain internal commas, so they must be separated by semicolons, matching the semicolon after "prey."

A.rationale: Because the items in the series already contain commas, a comma here makes the series hard to separate; the other items are divided by semicolons.

B.rationale: A colon cannot separate items within a series.

C.rationale: Without punctuation, the first two items run together.

hints: What separates the second and third items in the series?

strategy.explanation: Match the punctuation used between the other items.

candidates.remember: Use semicolons between series items that contain commas.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: which the beetle can aim in almost any direction
candidates.explanation: The subject "spray" is singular, so it takes "is"; the clause between the commas does not change the subject.

B.rationale: The subject is the singular "spray," not "direction" or "chambers."

C.rationale: "Being" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

D.rationale: The plural past-tense verb does not agree with the singular "spray."

hints: Which noun must the verb agree with?

strategy.explanation: Cross out the clause between the commas.

candidates.remember: Agree the verb with its subject, not with nouns in between.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: they can help keep downstream areas wet during droughts
candidates.explanation: Both parts are independent clauses, so a semicolon is needed before the transition "as a result," which is followed by a comma.

A.rationale: A comma before "as a result" creates a comma splice, since both parts are independent clauses.

C.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

D.rationale: "As a result" needs a comma after it, and a comma alone still cannot join the two clauses.

hints: Can both parts stand alone as sentences?

strategy.explanation: Treat "as a result" as a transition, not a conjunction.

candidates.remember: A transitional phrase cannot join clauses with only a comma.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Ants carry the seeds back to their nests, feed the elaiosomes to their larvae
candidates.explanation: The three verbs share the subject "Ants," so they must match: carry, feed, and discard.

A.rationale: The other verbs in the series are "carry" and "feed," so "discarding" breaks the parallel structure.

B.rationale: The past tense does not match the present-tense verbs "carry" and "feed."

C.rationale: An infinitive does not match "carry" and "feed."

hints: What form are the other verbs in the series?

strategy.explanation: Line up the verbs that share the subject.

candidates.remember: Items in a series should have the same grammatical form.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: light produced by colonies of a bacterium
candidates.explanation: The relative pronoun "that" refers to "colonies," which is plural, so the verb is "live."

A.rationale: "That" refers to the plural "colonies," so the verb must be plural.

B.rationale: The singular verb does not agree with the plural antecedent "colonies."

D.rationale: "Living" leaves the relative clause without a verb.

hints: What does "that" refer to, "colonies" or "bacterium"?

strategy.explanation: Find the antecedent of the relative pronoun.

candidates.remember: A relative pronoun takes the number of its antecedent.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: This yearly round trip is longer than
candidates.explanation: The comparison must be between trips: the tern's trip is longer than that (the trip) of any other animal.

B.rationale: "Those" is plural, but it stands for the singular "round trip."

C.rationale: "It" would compare the trip with itself.

D.rationale: "The ones" is plural and does not match the singular "round trip."

hints: What is being compared with what?

strategy.explanation: Make sure the two things compared are the same kind of thing.

candidates.remember: Compare like with like: use "that of" for a singular noun.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: many young artists of the Harlem Renaissance regarded as their mentor
candidates.explanation: Within the clause, "many young artists ... regarded her as their mentor," so the object form "whom" is correct.

A.rationale: The pronoun is the object of "regarded" (many young artists regarded her), so the object form is needed.

C.rationale: "Whose" shows possession, but nothing follows that Savage possesses.

hints: Would you say "artists regarded she" or "artists regarded her"?

strategy.explanation: Rearrange the clause to test the pronoun.

candidates.remember: Use "whom" where "her" or "him" would fit.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Joplin had arranged to receive a royalty of one cent on each copy sold
candidates.explanation: The subject of the clause is "sales," which is plural, so the plural past-tense verb "were" is correct.

A.rationale: The subject is the plural "sales," not "music."

C.rationale: The singular verb does not agree with "sales," and the tense shifts.

D.rationale: "Being" leaves the clause without a main verb.

hints: What is the subject of the second clause?

strategy.explanation: Cross out "of the sheet music."

candidates.remember: Agree the verb with its subject, not the nearest noun.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Lomax often asked the musicians where they had learned
candidates.explanation: "Where they had learned their songs" is an indirect question within a statement, so the sentence ends with a period.

A.rationale: The sentence reports a question indirectly, so it is a statement and ends with a period.

B.rationale: There is no direct quotation, so quotation marks and a question mark are wrong.

D.rationale: A sentence cannot end with a comma.

hints: Is the sentence asking a question or reporting one?

strategy.explanation: Decide whether the question is quoted directly.

candidates.remember: An indirect question ends with a period.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: without softening them
candidates.explanation: Painting her features "without softening them" means the portraits do not make her look more perfect than she was, so they are rarely "idealized."

A.rationale: Her portraits are frank, so they are often candid, not rarely candid.

C.rationale: Showing her own body and injuries makes the works deeply personal.

D.rationale: Nothing in the text suggests her portraits lack symbolism.

hints: What does "without softening them" tell you she did not do?

strategy.explanation: Predict a word meaning "made to look perfect."

candidates.remember: Use the evidence after the colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: Most earlier artists who depicted Cleopatra showed her in the moments before her death
candidates.explanation: Lewis broke from the usual way of depicting Cleopatra, so her approach was "unconventional."

B.rationale: The text says her approach departed from what earlier artists did, so it was not derivative.

C.rationale: Showing Cleopatra after death was the opposite of the usual approach.

D.rationale: Breaking with the usual depiction made her approach notable, not unremarkable.

hints: How did Lewis's choice compare with what most artists did?

strategy.explanation: Predict "unusual."

candidates.remember: Contrast words such as "instead" point to the meaning.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes a discovery and then explains why the discovery was later shown to be wrong.
choices.B: It compares two different orchids from Madagascar and explains how the flowers differ in structure.
choices.C: It presents a prediction, notes doubts about it, and then reports evidence that confirmed it.
choices.D: It explains how hawk moths feed and then argues that orchids depend entirely on them.

candidates.evidence: He predicted that some moth must have a tongue long enough to reach it
candidates.explanation: The text moves from Darwin's 1862 prediction, to doubts about it, to the 1903 description of a moth that fit it.

A.rationale: The 1903 description confirmed Darwin's prediction rather than disproving anything.

D.rationale: The text does not explain moth feeding in general or claim total dependence.

hints: What happens in 1862, and what happens in 1903?

strategy.explanation: Label each sentence's role.

candidates.remember: Structure answers must match every part of the text, in order.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Wright (Text 2) most likely respond to the explanation described in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the idea that the Sahara was ever covered by grasslands and lakes
choices.B: By claiming that herders, rather than orbital changes, were the sole cause of the drying
choices.C: By arguing that the monsoon rains actually grew stronger as the Sahara became drier
choices.D: By accepting that orbital changes drove the drying but arguing people may have hastened it

candidates.evidence: sped up the drying that was already under way
candidates.explanation: Wright says people "also" played a role and sped up drying that was already happening, so he accepts the orbital explanation while adding a human factor.

A.rationale: Wright does not dispute that the Sahara was once green.

B.rationale: Wright says people "also" played a role and sped up drying "already under way."

C.rationale: Text 2 says nothing about stronger monsoon rains.

hints: Does Wright replace the explanation in Text 1 or add to it?

strategy.explanation: Notice the words "also" and "already under way."

candidates.remember: Watch for answers that turn "also" into "only."

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a signature from Martinez increased what collectors were willing to pay for a pot.
choices.B: Martinez wanted to take credit for the work of other potters at San Ildefonso.
choices.C: collectors could not tell the difference between signed pottery and unsigned pottery.
choices.D: other potters at San Ildefonso had not learned to make black-on-black ware.

candidates.evidence: As collectors' interest grew, she began signing her pots
candidates.explanation: Martinez began signing pots as collectors' interest grew, and signing others' pots would help them only if her name added value for buyers.

B.rationale: The text gives no evidence of that motive; the practice is better explained by what a signature meant to buyers.

C.rationale: If collectors could not tell signed from unsigned pots, a signature would matter little.

D.rationale: The other women made pots that Martinez signed, so this does not follow.

hints: Why would a signature matter to the women whose pots she signed?

strategy.explanation: Connect the signing to the collectors mentioned earlier.

candidates.remember: An inference should be the most reasonable explanation the text supports.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Area 1 had 42 krill per cubic meter, the highest count of the three study areas.
choices.B: Krill counts rose from 6 to 18 to 42 as months of winter ice rose from 0 to 2 to 5.
choices.C: Area 3 had no sea ice the previous winter and had 6 krill per cubic meter that summer.
choices.D: Krill larvae feed on algae that grow on the underside of sea ice during the winter.

candidates.evidence: the longer an area had been covered by sea ice in winter, the more krill it had
candidates.explanation: The claim describes a trend across areas; only this choice shows krill counts increasing as months of ice increase.

A.rationale: This gives one area's count without showing the relationship across all three.

C.rationale: This describes only one area, so it cannot show a trend.

D.rationale: This explains a possible cause but does not use the data to show the pattern.

hints: Does the claim describe one area or a pattern across all of them?

strategy.explanation: Check whether each choice covers all three areas.

candidates.remember: A trend claim needs data from every group.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (finding that supports a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the ecologists' hypothesis?

choices.A: Palo verde trees produce seeds that birds and small mammals eat throughout the summer.
choices.B: Mature saguaros can grow taller than the palo verde trees that once sheltered them.
choices.C: Young saguaros under artificial shade cloth survived about as well as those beneath palo verdes.
choices.D: Young saguaros growing beneath palo verdes were more likely to survive than those growing in the open.

candidates.evidence: mainly by shading them from intense sunlight
candidates.explanation: If artificial shade alone gives the same benefit as a nurse plant, then shade is the main way the nurse plant helps.

A.rationale: This describes palo verdes but says nothing about how they help saguaros survive.

B.rationale: This describes later growth, not what helps young saguaros survive.

D.rationale: This shows nurse plants help but does not show that shade, rather than something else, is the reason.

hints: Which finding isolates shade from everything else a tree provides?

strategy.explanation: Look for a result that tests the specific cause.

candidates.remember: The strongest support isolates the cause the hypothesis names.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: the league's power had begun to fade
candidates.explanation: The text moves from the league's dominance to its decline, so a contrast transition is needed.

A.rationale: The league's decline was not caused by its privileges.

B.rationale: The decline is not similar to the league's earlier dominance; it contrasts with it.

C.rationale: The decline is not another advantage of the league.

hints: Does the last sentence continue or reverse the earlier picture?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before choosing.

candidates.remember: Use "However" to signal a contrast.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: applying a single color to every panel where it was needed
candidates.explanation: Applying each color across all sixty panels produced the series' consistent colors, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.

A.rationale: The unity follows from his method; it is not a contrast.

C.rationale: The visual unity is not an example of his method; it is a result of it.

D.rationale: The unity did not happen at the same time as something else; it resulted from the method.

hints: Did the method cause the unity or contrast with it?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before choosing.

candidates.remember: Use "As a result" for an effect that follows from a cause.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize that formal recognition from the Pulitzer board came to Ellington only long after it was first proposed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Duke Ellington, who led one of the most celebrated orchestras in American music, composed more than a thousand works.
choices.B: In 1999, twenty-five years after Duke Ellington's death, the Pulitzer board awarded him a special citation for his work.
choices.C: Though a Pulitzer jury recommended honoring Ellington in 1965, the board did not award him a citation until 1999.
choices.D: Ellington composed "Mood Indigo" in 1930, more than three decades before a Pulitzer jury recommended a special award for him.

candidates.evidence: the Pulitzer board declined to give it
candidates.explanation: Only this choice includes both the 1965 recommendation and the 1999 citation, which together show the long delay.

A.rationale: This describes his career but not the delay in recognition.

B.rationale: This gives the 1999 award but not the earlier proposal, so it does not show how long recognition was delayed.

D.rationale: This links 1930 to 1965 but does not mention the board's eventual citation.

hints: Which choice includes both when recognition was proposed and when it came?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against both parts of the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must meet every part of the goal.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain the significance of Leavitt's discovery to an audience unfamiliar with Cepheid stars. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, who worked at the Harvard College Observatory in the early 1900s, studied Cepheid variable stars, which brighten and dim on a regular, repeating cycle.
choices.B: In 1912, Henrietta Swan Leavitt reported that the brighter Cepheid variable stars in her study at the Harvard College Observatory had longer cycles than the dimmer ones did.
choices.C: Leavitt found that brighter Cepheids, stars that brighten and dim on a regular cycle, have longer cycles, which gave astronomers a way to measure distances to faraway galaxies.
choices.D: In the 1920s, the astronomer Edwin Hubble used Cepheid variable stars, which brighten and dim on a regular cycle, to show that some galaxies lie far beyond the Milky Way.

candidates.evidence: a Cepheid's cycle reveals its true brightness
candidates.explanation: Only this choice tells an unfamiliar audience what a Cepheid is and why Leavitt's finding mattered: it made it possible to measure distances to faraway galaxies.

A.rationale: This describes what Leavitt studied but not why her discovery mattered.

B.rationale: This states the finding but does not explain its significance to an unfamiliar audience.

D.rationale: This describes Hubble's work without connecting it to Leavitt's discovery.

hints: Which choice says why the discovery mattered?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must accomplish the stated goal.

revision_history.reason: blind solver B: key did not explain what a Cepheid is for an unfamiliar audience, and it credited Leavitt alone with showing that the cycle reveals true brightness
revision_history.change: key now defines Cepheids, states her actual 1912 finding, and gives its significance
